hints: Notice the $12\text{ k}\Omega$ resistor is between the middle point and $0\text{ V}$, so $1.0\text{ V}$ across it leaves $5.0\text{ V}$ across $R$.
In series the current $I$ is the same, so use $V = IR$ to see that voltage is proportional to resistance.
Set up the ratio $V_R/V_{12} = R/12\text{ k}\Omega$ with $V_R = 5.0\text{ V}$ and $V_{12} = 1.0\text{ V}$ and solve for $R$.
walkthrough: The $6.0\text{ V}$ supply is shared by the series pair $R$ and $12\text{ k}\Omega$, so $V_R + V_{12} = 6.0\text{ V}$.
Required $V_{12} = 1.0\text{ V}$, so the p.d. across $R$ must be $V_R = 6.0 - 1.0 = 5.0\text{ V}$.
The same current $I$ flows through both, so $V_R = IR$ and $V_{12} = I \times 12\text{ k}\Omega$.
Divide to remove $I$: $V_R/V_{12} = R/12\text{ k}\Omega$, so $5.0/1.0 = R/12\text{ k}\Omega$.
Hence $R = 5.0 \times 12\text{ k}\Omega = 60\text{ k}\Omega$. This is option C.

options.A: A $2.0\text{ k}\Omega$ resistor would drop much less than $5.0\text{ V}$, so the $12\text{ k}\Omega$ resistor would get almost all of the $6.0\text{ V}$.
options.B: With $10\text{ k}\Omega$ the two resistances are similar, so the $12\text{ k}\Omega$ resistor would get about half of $6.0\text{ V}$, not $1.0\text{ V}$.
options.C: With $R = 60\text{ k}\Omega$ the voltage divides as $5.0\text{ V}$ to $1.0\text{ V}$, matching the $5:1$ resistance ratio $60\text{ k}\Omega : 12\text{ k}\Omega$.
options.D: A $72\text{ k}\Omega$ resistor gives total $84\text{ k}\Omega$, so the $12\text{ k}\Omega$ share is $(12/84) \times 6.0\text{ V} < 1.0\text{ V}$.
